newsitem.title: USA: U.S experts eye fresh cracks in Euro currency plan.
newsitem.headline: U.S experts eye fresh cracks in Euro currency plan.

text.p: Fresh questions about Europe's plan to introduce a single currency by 1999 have emerged in the wake of recent German economic data, sparking renewed skepticism but little surprise among U.S. observers.

Cracks began to surface early this month after shockingly weak German employment figures for January spurred doubts about Germany's ability to meet strict Maastricht criteria in time for Economic and Monetary Union entry.

And while Germany's government has stuck steadfastly to seemingly optimistic growth forecasts for 1997, the country's stubborn jobless crisis has led even members of Chancellor Helmut Kohl's own Christian Democratic party to question the leadership of Europe's top euro-champion.

Suddenly, after months of optimism, Germany's problems have brought the contentious debate over who will qualify in the first stage of EMU to the forefront and raised eyebrows on the other side of the Atlantic.

"Recent employment numbers have raised questions about Germany's ability to meet Maastricht criteria on the deficit and debt without additional measures being taken," said Marc Chandler, currency strategist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in New York.

"Our view remains that the greatest likelihood is that a narrow group of core European countries will get together to form EMU on time but there has been, on the margins, some increased concern about Germany," he added.

German unemployment surged by over half a million to a new postwar record of 4.7 million in January, reaching levels last seen in the Great Depression of the 1930s. The unemployment rate, based on unadjusted data, advanced to 12.2 percent.

Amid repeated reaffirmations of Germany's commitment to EMU from government officials, Germany's central bank said on Wednesday that the country's chances of meeting single currency criteria will depend on how Bonn overcomes pressures from record unemployment.

Double-digit jobless rates forced the government to pay out unexpected billions of marks in benefits, swelling Germany's budget deficit to 3.9 percent of Gross Domestic Product in 1996 -- well above the 3.0 percent target required in 1997 for entry into the currency union.

And earlier this week Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi took the unprecedented step of lashing out at Europe's top economic power, forcefully questioning Germany's political leadership for failing to take necessary action to prepare its economy for monetary union.
Encouraging business confidence data from Germany's respected Ifo economics institute acted as a reminder on Thursday that all is not gloomy in the German economy.
The dollar has risen over 10 percent against the mark since the beginning of the year, offering some glimmer of hope for export-led German growth.
But clearly Germany's problems have once again spurred EMU doubts that were largely absent during the latter part of 1996.

"All these questions have been around for a long time, but I think that now there will be some more opportunity to trade the other way and bet against EMU," said Chris Iggo, chief economist at BZW Securities Inc.

"As we get closer to the deadlines the rhetoric will grow more intense, the divisions within Europe are going to become more obvious and the difficulties of meeting the targets will come to the front of the market's thinking," he predicted.
Although economists expect doubts to multiply in the months ahead, many remain confident of the political commitment to Europe's currency plan.
U.S. credit rating agency Moody's Investors Service said on Thursday that it was highly probable European economic and monetary union would start on time.
"There's a strong dynamic pushing the process forward," David Levey, co-head of Moody's sovereign risk unit, told Reuters on Thursday.

Levey said Moody's was currently "pretty certain" that Finland and Belgium would be two of eight countries in the first wave of EMU. The others would likely be Austria, France, Germany, Netherlands, Ireland and Luxembourg.

But Carl Weinberg, chief economist at advisory firm High Frequency Economics, echoed a number of other U.S. economists who said it was difficult to predict at this stage just when EMU will occur and which countries will be its founding members.
"I'm advising all my clients to bet on volatiltity, but I'm not going to tell them to make a directional play because I can't see any basis on which to make those predictions," he said.
((-- N.A. Treasury Desk 212-859-1660))
